Don't know about Mint, haven't used it in ages, but I installed Manjaro OpenRC Fluxbox on my 3 year old AMD laptop as simple as deleting all Windows partitions via GParted and installing the system. Just download Rufus from https://rufus.akeo.ie/ to make a live USB and you'd be good to go. Most distros come with GParted already on their live versions so I assume it's the same for Mint.

Er, I'm not sure what exactly you're asking here. I think you've made some assumptions that maybe aren't accurate. So, I'll just go through your questions in order as best as I can. ASUS ROG models came out starting in 06, so you are almost certainly on a GPT drive with UEFI. If you were on MBR, that would not matter for linux, just repartition the whole drive and go. Since you're probably on GPT, it still doesn't matter, just repartition and go. If you were using oldschool BIOS, that would matter for GPT, but I HIGHLY doubt you are. Even if you do have BIOS instead of UEFI for some reason, Linux works with that as well.

"If it's MBR then Linux is verboten as the system recovery partition cannot be deleted." This I don't understand. I could and did remove my Windows recovery partition when I switched to full linux. I don't see any reason why anyone would want to keep a windows recovery partition eating up space on a linux box anyway.

"If it's GPT then Linux and the creation of new partitions is the solution" Unless you intend to dual boot, nuking the disk and installing linux alone is the solution. If you DO want to dual boot, GPT/MBR makes no difference.

Assuming no dual boot: Nuke the drive and install linux with a small partition for swap

Assuming dual boot: Nuke the recovery partition (That shit's full of OEM bloatware anyway), DON'T nuke the windows UEFI boot partition, Install Linux on your new 4th primary partition (if MBR, GPT doesn't have that 4 primary limitation iirc), leave Windows where it is, and be sure to update grub so windows shows up in your boot menu.

I am now dual booting Linux Mint 17.2 and Windows 8.1. Another responder verified that my drive is UEFI and supports multiple (greater than four partitions). Creating new Linux partitions is possible.

Creating new partitions on a BIOS MBR drive is a nightmare. Primary, secondary, logical partition structures dance in my head like clouds of a hurricane. I.e. I don't like it so won't invest time to resolve the issue.
